catalog_quote: (16) Syllabic Maximality (SYL ≤ µµ): Banawá syllables are maximally bimoraic. ... As originally described in BBE, Banawá stresses every other mora from left-to-right within the word, skipping word-initial vowels in words with more than two syllables. The words in (46) illustrate the basic stress rule: (46) a. súirì 'penis' b. wárabù 'ear' c. wánakàri 'spider' d. yífuyà 'fire' e. uwárià 'one' f. úwi 'cry' ... its basic stress pattern is indeed a common left-to-right moraic trochaic system. ... (47) Foot Binarity (FTBIN): Feet are binary (on moras). (48) ALIGN FT: (FT, L, PRWD, L) ... Feet are bimoraic in Banawá with the exception of word-final, monomoraic feet in words of odd-numbered moras (omitting word-initial vowels). ... (69) ... e. máka rì 'cloth' ... its degenerate feet are neither restricted to "strong position", i.e. to where primary stress falls (see (69) above), nor are they completely unrestricted ... (83) a. kèrewéduàma 'turn end over end' b. (ke re) (wedu)(a ma) ... (84) a. tìkadámuèi 'you forget' b. (ti ka)(da mu)(uei) ... whereas Banawá diphthongs are all bimoraic, Suruwahá has only light, monomoraic diphthongs ... Suruwahá thus has syllabic iambs, whereas Banawá has moraic trochees. Interestingly, it is Suruwahá's iambic system which has lost the distinction between light and heavy syllables. This distinction has been maintained in the moraic, trochaic systems in Banawá. ... a result of the fact that SYLLINT is violated in Banawá foot construction
sweep_summary: Two title-hits for jama1261 (Madi; both actually about the Banawá variety, bana1307). (1) Buller, Buller & Everett 1993 (IJAL 59(3):280-293, DOI 10.1086/466199): open author copy on daneverettbooks. it is the original first-hand description that the catalog's current deciding source (Everett 1996 ROA-121) restates, and it confirms the weight coding (CV/CVV only, one mora per vowel, stress every other vowel L->R within the word, initial vowel extraprosodic except in bimoraic words, tautosyllabic vowels may belong to different feet) while adding, in n. 5, the hedged primary-stress rule (penultimate stress-bearing vowel, 'numerous exceptions') that Everett 1996 lacks in prose; recommended as the citation of record, with Everett 1996 kept for the degenerate-foot and diphthong-weight detail. (2) Wiltshire 2004, MA thesis (University of Manchester, 71 pp.) on stress in connected speech in Banawá: no online copy found (Glottolog record has no URL; Manchester Library Search returns 0 local hits for it; medium acquisition priority (first-hand, but phrase-level, and unlikely to displace BBE 1993). for the session was exhausted; all look-ups were done with direct download/automated download. Saved files and are under Manchester Library Search also surfaced two theoretical reanalyses of the BBE data not in the item list (Hyde, 'Issues in Banawá Prosody', LI; Martínez-Paricio & Kager, LI note on Banawá grid vs. metrical structure), not downloaded.

new_statements.reading: Banawá (Madi) has iterative left-to-right binary left-headed (trochaic) feet built over vowels/moras within the grammatical word: every odd-numbered nucleus from the left is stressed, a word-initial vowel is extraprosodic (unstressed) in words of more than two vowels but stressed in bimoraic words (minimality), syllables are CV or CVV with one mora per vowel and feet may split a CVV syllable. Primary stress is only tentatively assigned (footnote): generally the penultimate stress-bearing vowel, with many exceptions. This is the peer-reviewed, first-hand description by the resident fieldworkers (the Bullers, ~six years with the Banawá; 1989 SIL corpus) that Everett 1996 restates; it confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding (CVV = two moras, mora-counting trochees) and supplies the primary-stress statement the current deciding source lacks in prose.

Extraprosodic sounds, by definition, are not stressed and are not included in this stress pattern, for example if a word begins with an extraprosodic vowel then this syllable is not counted and stress is applied to the second syllable and every other syllable after that (Buller, Buller & Everett 1993:287). new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Everett 1996 ROA-121, classification weight: maximally bimoraic syllables, left-to-right moraic trochees skipping a word-initial vowel in longer words) and with the statement held by the project from Buller, Buller & Everett 1993, which it restates as undisputed for words in isolation (pp.5-6, 9: 'the facts proposed in this article are not disputable'). It adds connected-speech detail not on record: the alternating count can run across word boundaries, phrase-medial word-initial vowels may be stressed, CVV always stressed, acoustic ranking duration > amplitude > pitch, explicit statement that Banawá is not tonal. It does not propose a different word-stress pl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wiltshire takes over Buller, Buller & Everett's (1993) word-level system as established and undisputed for isolated words: syllables are CV or CVV, each vowel one mora; stress every other vowel (mora) left to right in trochaic (strong-weak) feet; word-initial onsetless vowels (in words of three or more moras) and word-final /i/ are extraprosodic, so a vowel-initial longer word stresses its second vowel and alternates from there; CVV (two-mora) syllables always carry a stress. Her own contribution, from Praat analysis of one passage of connected speech by one speaker recorded by Everett: in running speech the alternation often continues across word and morpheme boundaries (constraint 'Swsw: stress every other vowel from left to right, ignoring word and morpheme boundaries'), phrase-medial word-initial vowels can be stressed (Swsw >> EXMET) while phrase-initial ones are not (ALIGN S-L), CVV syllables attract stress (CVVSTRESS >> Swsw), every word carries a stress (WORDSTRESS), no more than two adjacent syllables share the same stress value (*+2STRESS), plus ad hoc constraints CV=CV and *NASAL for residual cases; acoustically, vowel/syllable duration is the strongest correlate of stress, then amplitude, with pitch (maximum F0) playing a role only when length and amplitude do not decide; Banawá is stated not to be a tonal language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentions primary vs secondary only in passing (p.45: 'diphthongs are always stressed in some way, whether primary or secondary'; p.43: word-final CVV carries the greatest amplitude but 'other factors will play a role in signifying primary stress such as vowel duration'); no rule for locating primary stress among the stressed vowels is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Connected-speech departures from the isolated-word rule: stress shift to avoid stressing two word-initial vowels (ex. 6b u'da'dusi 'kuma: u'da'dusi 'te:ne 'bisa:), stressed word-initial extraprosodic vowel phrase-medially (ex. 8b 'jama 'eki'ja:), unstressed CVV /tai/ in i'ma 'ki: tai da'rame (ex. 40), syllables with a nasal onset tending to be unstressed (ma'ka ma'ka; u'dainu'ku 'hama), sequences with /w/ unexplained ('tuwa'wisa follows Swsw); author stresses the data are one passage from one speaker.
new_statements.identity_note: Banawá proper (the Banawá dialect of Madi, c. 70 speakers, Amazonas, Brazil); data = one passage of connected speech from one (male) speaker recorded in the field by Daniel Everett, transcribed and measured in Praat by the author; isolated-word facts are taken from Buller, Buller & Everett 1993 and Ladefoged, Ladefoged & Everett 1997.

tone_statements.citation: Everett, Daniel L. and Ladefoged, Peter and Ladefoged, Jenny (1997). Phonetic structures of Banawa, an endangered language. Phonetica 54. pp. 94-111.
tone_statements.quote: Banawá has a very simple suprasegmental structure. Neither tone nor length play any role in distinguishing words, and stress is entirely predictable. Stress in Banawá occurs on the first mora in a word, and on every other mora after the first. The only exceptions to this rule are words with three or more moras beginning with a vowel. In such words the onsetless first vowel is not counted as a mora in the stress assignment process. A formal statement of the stress rule would embody two additional constraints: (6) An initial vowel in a word cannot form a mora in words with three or more moras. (7) Stress occurs on alternate moras within a word, beginning with the first mora.

Fill the primary-stress field: 'primary stress on the penultimate stressed vowel (rightmost non-final foot head); never on the word-final mora' from held BBE 1993 fn.5 p.288 and MP&K 2020 pp.169,173 (edge: right-oriented main stress over L-to-R alternating count). Add a caution that the system counts vowels/moras and splits CVV syllables, so some analysts (MP&K 2020:169) label it 'quantity-insensitive rhythmic stress on alternating vowels'; CVV counts as two positions, which is what the 'weight / CVV' coding encodes.

sources.citation: Hyde, Brett. 2007. Issues in Banawá Prosody: Onset Sensitivity, Minimal Words, and Syllable Integrity. Linguistic Inquiry 38(2): 239-285. doi:10.1162/ling.2007.38.2.239
sources.quote: when a form has an initial CV or CVV syllable, its stress pattern is trochaic. Stress occurs on every odd-numbered mora counting from the left. [...] when a form has an initial V syllable, its stress pattern is iambic. Stress occurs on every even-numbered mora counting from the left. [...] In forms long enough to contain two or more stressed moras, the primary stress is the penultimate stress, indicating that primary stress prefers to occur over the penultimate foot, rather than the final foot.
sources.locator: pp. 239-240 (intro, exx. (1)-(2)); p. 244 ('primary stress never occurs on a prosodic word-final mora'); p. 275 (sec. 5, primary stress)

The work describes Jarawara, which Vogel treats as a sister dialect of Banawá within Madi, not Banawá itself; the even/odd mora-parity alternation in the phonological word is compatible with (and indirectly supports) the left-to-right mora-counting trochaic analysis in the existing Buller, Buller & Everett 1993 statement but says nothing about stress placement.

tone.quote: The overall pitch contour in Banawá shows very little variation in profiles. Syllables, whether accented or not, usually have falling pitch or in some rare cases stay level or rise. Accented syllables with pitch prominence are always high, never low, which allows us to predict the following two pitch movements: one with a jump up to the accented syllable and one with a jump down from the accented syllable. [...] Pitch accent in Banawá is used to indicate focus relations and contrast in combination with certain morphosyntactic means.
tone.locator: sec. 3.1 'Profiles', p. 19; sec. 4 Conclusion, p. 48 (word-stress restatement: sec. 2.3, p. 18; pitch vs stress mismatch: sec. 3.3.3, p. 27)
tone.summary: No lexical tone described: pitch functions intonationally (high pitch accents on stressed syllables marking focus/contrast, falling 'profile 1' vs rising 'profile 2'), on top of predictable trochaic word stress counted from the left edge.
